questions.question_text: Which statement correctly describes a **planar** graph?

options.text: A graph that can be drawn with no two edges crossing.
A graph in which no two edges cross in the drawing you have been given.
options.why: Makes planarity a property of one picture; a planar graph is often first drawn with crossings in it.

options.text: A graph drawn with all of its vertices lying on one straight line.
options.why: Confuses being planar with a flat arrangement of the vertices, which has nothing to do with crossings.

options.text: A graph in which every face is bounded by the same number of edges.
options.why: Invents a condition about the shape of the faces instead of asking whether the edges can avoid crossing.

questions.solution_text:
Planar describes the network, not one picture of it.
The test is whether some arrangement of the same vertices and edges has no crossings.
**A graph that can be drawn with no two edges crossing.**

options.text: Yes — the same vertices and tracks can be rearranged so that nothing crosses.
No — two tracks cross in the drawing, so the graph is non-planar.
options.why: Judges the picture instead of the network; a graph is non-planar only when every possible drawing has a crossing.

options.text: No — a crossing can only be removed by deleting one of the tracks.
options.why: Assumes a redraw has to lose an edge, when moving the vertices keeps all of them and clears the crossings.

options.text: Yes — but only once the vertex $E$ is removed from the network.
options.why: A redraw must keep every vertex; removing $E$ produces a different graph, not a redrawing of this one.

questions.solution_text:
The crossings come from where the vertices have been placed, not from the network itself.
Drawing the ring $A$–$B$–$C$–$D$ with the track $AC$ inside it leaves $B$ and $D$ on the outside, so the path $D$–$E$–$B$ can be taken right around the outside with no crossing.
**Yes — the graph is planar.**

options.text: It still has $6$ vertices and $8$ tracks, and no two tracks cross.
It has $6$ vertices and $7$ tracks, because removing the crossing removes a track.
options.why: Treats the crossing point as belonging to a track that can be deleted; a redraw moves tracks but never loses one.

options.text: It has $7$ vertices and $10$ tracks, because the crossing point becomes a new component.
options.why: Turns the crossing into a vertex and splits both tracks through it in two, which invents connections that do not exist.

options.text: It cannot be redrawn, because a drawing containing a crossing is always non-planar.
options.why: Reads planarity off one drawing; here the track $BF$ can simply be taken around the outside.

questions.solution_text:
A redraw must keep exactly the same vertices and exactly the same tracks — only their positions on the page change.
Taking the track $BF$ around the outside of the ring leaves the track $AD$ inside, and nothing crosses.
**It still has $6$ vertices and $8$ tracks, and no two tracks cross.**

options.text: No — Drawing 2 joins $B$ and $D$ where Drawing 1 joined $A$ and $C$.
Yes — Drawing 2 has the same six tracks and no crossings.
options.why: Counts the tracks without checking which pairs they join; one track has been moved onto a different pair of components.

options.text: No — Drawing 2 has only five tracks, so one has been deleted.
options.why: Sees that $AC$ is gone but misses the new chord $BD$, so counts five tracks in Drawing 2 instead of six.

options.text: No — two of the tracks in Drawing 2 still cross.
options.why: Misreads Drawing 2, in which the chord $BD$ lies inside the ring and crosses nothing.

questions.solution_text:
Drawing 1 joins $AB$, $BC$, $CD$, $DE$, $EA$, $AC$.
Drawing 2 joins $AB$, $BC$, $CD$, $DE$, $EA$, $BD$.
Both have six tracks and Drawing 2 has no crossings, but the sixth track now joins a different pair of components, so it is a drawing of a different circuit.
**No — the redraw has not succeeded.**

options.why: Counts the five regions fenced in by tracks and leaves out the unbounded region outside the drawing.
Counts the five inner regions and the outer region, then adds one more for the hub $H$ as though a vertex were a face.
Gives the number of tracks instead of the number of regions the tracks cut the page into.

questions.solution_text:
The five spokes from $H$ cut the inside of the ring into five regions.
The unbounded region outside the ring is one more face.
$5+1$
$=6$
**The drawing has $6$ faces.**

options.why: Treats the loop as fencing nothing in, counting only the two halves of the square and the outer region.
Counts the loop as creating two regions, one on each side of it, when it encloses just one.
Counts only the two regions the diagonal $BD$ makes, forgetting both the loop's region and the outer region.

questions.solution_text:
The diagonal $BD$ cuts the square into two regions.
The loop at $A$ fences in one more region, and the unbounded outside region is a face as well.
$2+1+1$
$=4$
**The drawing has $4$ faces.**

options.text: There are $4$ faces; the unbounded region outside the plan has not been numbered.
There are $3$ faces; every face of the drawing has already been numbered.
options.why: Leaves out the outer region, which is always counted as a face — the commonest slip in face counting.

options.text: There are $3$ faces; the outer region is not a face because nothing bounds it on the outside.
options.why: Spots the outer region but wrongly rules it out; a face need not be enclosed on all sides to be counted.

options.text: There are $4$ faces; the strip between regions $1$ and $2$ has not been numbered.
options.why: Invents a region along the doorway $AC$, where regions $1$ and $2$ simply share a boundary.

questions.solution_text:
Regions $1$, $2$ and $3$ are the three regions fenced in by doorways.
The region stretching away outside the whole plan is also a face and has no number.
$3+1$
$=4$
**There are $4$ faces; the unbounded outer region has not been numbered.**

options.text: No — it is $K_5$, one of the two standard non-planar graphs.
Yes — the rooms can be moved around until none of the doorways cross.
options.why: Assumes every tangle can be undone by moving vertices, which fails for the two standard non-planar graphs.

options.text: Yes — the crossings disappear if the doorways are drawn as curves instead of straight lines.
options.why: Curving edges changes the picture but not the network, so a non-planar graph still keeps a crossing.

options.text: No — but only because $10$ doorways will not fit on a single page.
options.why: Blames the number of edges and the space available rather than the structure of the network.

questions.solution_text:
Each of the five rooms is joined to all four of the others, so the network is $K_5$.
$K_5$ is non-planar, so every drawing of it has at least one crossing.
**No — the graph is not planar.**

options.why: Assumes a track drawn inside an existing region leaves the number of regions unchanged.
Counts the new track as creating two extra regions rather than dividing one region into two.
Counts only the two halves of the square, ignoring the triangle $DEC$ and the outer region.

questions.solution_text:
Before the new track there are two enclosed regions — the square and the triangle $DEC$ — plus the outer region, giving $3$ faces.
The track $AC$ is drawn inside the square, so it divides that one region into $ABC$ and $ACD$.
$3+1$
$=4$
**The new drawing has $4$ faces.**
